Delhi Schools Associated with Health Care Programmes 
*481. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether schools in Delhi are associated with various health care and 
awareness programmes viz. Health Related Information Dissemination Amongst 
Youth (HRI- DAY), Student Health Action Network (SHAN), School Charter on 
Health Of Our Land (SCHOOL), School Annual Health Report Programme 
(SHARP); 
(b) if so, whether Government would introduce such programmes through-
out the country, especially in metros; 
(c) if so, by when; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI): (a) Yes, Sir. Occasiona l symposia/meetings in 
regard to the health awareness programmes referred to in the question have 
been held by the voluntary organisations in some schools of Delhi. 
(b) to (d) There is no such proposal with this Ministry.

Statement 
(a) In pursuance of Minimum Support Price (MSP) operations during 
kharif 1994-95 in Punjab, the State Agencies procured some paddy. The State 
Agencies could not get the paddy milled, and which had to be consequently 
auctioned. A sum of Rs. 120 crores, being the difference between the cost of

final settlement. The claim of loss of Rs. 8.19 crores and Rs. 10.48 crores in 
M.S.P. operation pertaining to wheat for Rabi 1993- 94 and 1995- 96 
respectively was rejected on the grounds that the responsibility for storage and 
preservation of procured stocks is that of the State Agencies, prior to the 
handing over of these stocks to the Food Corporation of India.

*499. SHRIE.BALANANDAN: 
SHRIGULAM NABI AZAD: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the scientific forum has challenged the ongoing programme 
of HIV/AIDS; 
(b) whether Government have ordered review of second phase of  HIV/ 
AIDS programme; 
(c) if so, whether the process has been started 
(d) whether any International Conference was field at Nagpur to ascertain 
validity of HIV/AIDS programme, including methods of testing; 
(e) if so, the particulars of participants, including international experts 
from foreign countries, broad features of the agenda discussed and the outcome 
thereof; and 
(0 the action initiated by Government to redress the victims of the 
programme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) to(f) The ongoing National 
AIDS Control Programme Phase -II has been formulated after extensive 
consultations with State Governments, concerned Ministries in the Govt. of 
India, NGOs and representatives of civil society. The programme was thereafter 
approved by the Union Cabinet in August, 1999. No scientific forum has 
challenged the ongoing Programme nor has the Government issued any order 
for its review. 
The President, Academy of Nutrition Improvement, Nagpur, had organised 
an International Conference on the validity of HIV/AIDS Programme, including 
methods of testing at Nagpur on 30th & 31st January, 2000. The Conference 
was attended by fifty participants including representative from WHO, ICMR 
and some delegates from abroad. 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2000] 
The agenda discussed was: (i) Validity of HIV strains prevalent in India 
and different parts of the World; (ii) Methods of diagnosis of HIV infection; 
(iii) HIV infection as the cause of AIDS. 
Some of the participants were of the view that the causative agent of 
AIDS i.e. the Human Immuno-deficiency Virus has not been identified and that 
there are other diseases which give a false positive test for HIV. The representative 
from ICMR clarified that several strains of HIV has been iso lated in India and 
elswhere in the world. The present available HIV testing kits are highly sensitive 
and specific for detection HIV infection and false positive results do not occur 
at any significant level, provided the procedure for testing is correctly followed. 
As far as the efficacy of antiretroviral drugs in prevention of mother to child 
transmission is concerned. It has been scientifically proved to be an effective 
way to prevent HIV transmission in newborns. 
It was the impression of representatives of ICMR and WHO that some of 
the participants had biased opinions which were not scientifically sound and 
did not know much about national and international scientific status of HIV 
research. 
Also, it is a well established scientific conclusion that HIV is the causative 
organism for AIDS.

Food Deficiency and Maternal Mortality in India 
3666. SHRI SURESH KALMADI: 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite a substantial increase in foodgrains 
production during the 50 years of independence, half the world's hungry people 
are in India which is still classified by the Food and Agriculture Organisation as 
a "low income and food-deficit country"; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that maternal mortality rate among the Indian 
women is one of the highest in the world; and 
45 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2000] 
(c) if so, the steps Government plan to overcome this problem? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) 
According to a FAO publication people who do not have enough to eat are termed 
as "undernourished". As per FAO, around 790 million people in developing 
world and 34 million in developed world are undernourished. Regarding India, the 
number of undernourished people has been estimated at 204.4 million by FAO. 
However, as per the Ninth Plan document of Planning Commission, percentage of 
persons without two square meals a day for some months of the year is often termed 
as the "hunger ratio". As per our Ninth Plan document, about 19 percent of the rural 
population and 7 percent of the urban population remained hungry in 1983 and, as per 
the latest available information, these have come down to about 5 percent in rural areas 
and 2 percent in urban areas in 1993-94. 
(b) There are no regular and comparable data available on maternal 
mortality ratio in India. The Sample registration Survey 1997 estimated the maternal 
mortality ratio at 408 per one lakh live birth. This is one of the highest in the world. 
(c) The Department of Family Welfare is currently implementing the 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme which aims at reducing the maternal 
mortality and morbidity in India. Through this programme, it endeavours to provide 
essential and emergency obstretic care, promote institutional deliveries, promote safe 
domiciliary deliveries through trained and traditional birth attendants, providing 
referral transportation for pregnant women, improving access to safe abortion 
services and introduce treatment for reproductive track infection, sexually 
transmitted infection and prophelaxis against nutritional anaemia.

Sugar Scam 
3672. SHRI VAYALAR RAVI: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the  news item 
published in the Indian Express on February 2,2000 under the caption "Another 
Sugar scam in the offing"; and 
(b) if so, what are the details in this regard and the reasons to overrule the 
concerned Ministry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) The news item published in the Indian Express on 
February 2, 2000 under the caption "Another Sugar Scam in the offing" 
mentioned about the addtional freesale sugar quota give n by the Government 
over and above the normal freesale quota. Consequent upon the publication of 
the above news item, the Government have already clarified the position as 
under: 
"Government has done away with ad -hoc allotment of additional 
quantities to s ugar mills, on a purely discretionary basis, over and above the 
pro-rata allotment to sugar mills out of the monthly releases of sugar in the 
freesale. This new policy has come into effect from Its January, 2000. 
However, certain sugar mills have represent ed to Government that on 
account of non-sanction of working capital by banks, they are having problems 
in settling the dues to the farmers especially during the peak crushing season. 
Farmers in these areas have been agitated over non-payment of their dues while 
sugar mills have been producing sugar and stocking them. Taking into account 
these practical problems, Government have decided to make exceptions in a 
very few cases to make advance additional allotments during the crushing 
season to such mills within their over -all yearly entitlement for release. Clear 
guidelines have been laid down to restrict the number to a few mills who have 
problems of working capital. Also it has been decided to make these advance 
releases only for a few months during the crushing season and these are spread 
over both freesale and levy entitlements. The disbursement of money to the 
farmers towards cane price dues from the realisation and sale of these additional 
quantities will also be monitored on month-to-month basis. The advance releases 
will also be adjusted at the same rate immediately after the crushing season. It 
is to be noted that advance allotments are made during the season when prices 
51 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2000] 
in the open market are under control and the mills do not have any undue 
advantage over other mills. The actual allotment of sugar will be made by the 
Department of Sugar and Edible Oils on exmination of representations from 
sugar mills received. Reference to PMO or involvement of PMO in any other 
way does not arise. 
It is, therefore, clarified that Government has not restored the system of 
additional allotments to sugar mills. Only advance allotments are being made 
in certain exceptional cases."

Conversion of one third land of the country into forests 
3690. SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA: 
DR. D. MASTHAN: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT A ND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether any scheme has been formulated by the Government to convert 
l/3rd land of the country into forest land; 
(b) if so, the details of the scheme. 
(c) whether any assessment has been made regarding the expenditure to 
be incurred on implementations of this scheme has been made; and 
76 

[28 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, the details of the amount and the time-limit fixed for converting 
the land into forest land? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) Yes, Sir. The Ministry of 
Environment & Forests have formulated National Forestry Action Programme 
(NFAP), a comprehensive strategic long term plan for the next twenty years to 
bring one third of the area of the country under tree cover and to arrest-forestation 
for achieving sustainable development of forests. 
(b) The National Forestry Action Programme has live main programmes: 
I. Protect Existing Forest Resources: It has three main -sub programmes 
(i) forest protection, (ii) soil and water conservation, and (iii) protected areas  
and biodiversity conservation. 
II. Improve Forest Productivity: It has four main sub -programmes. (i) 
rehabilitation of degraded forests, (ii) research and technology development, (iii) 
development of Non Wood Forest Products and (iv) assisting private 
initiative with community participation. 
III. Reduce Total Demand: It has three main sub programmes for the 
efficient uses of (i) fuelwood and fodder, (ii) timber, and (iii) Non Wood Forest 
Products. 
IV. Strengthen Policy and Institutional Framework: It has three main sub 
programmes (i) Central forestry administration, (ii) Central forestry 
institutions, and (iii) State forestry administration and institutions. 
V. Expand Forest Area: It has two main sub -programmes, (i) tree 
plantation on forest and non -forest land, and (ii) people's participation in 
plantations and its protection. 
(c) and (d) The implementation of NFAP requires huge financial resources 
and it is estimated that Rs. 1339 billions would be required in the next tw enty 
years to bring one third of the area of the country under tree cover. The programme 
will be implemented by the States/UTs. The present document aims at sustainable 
development of 76.5 million ha. of forests covering 16 major forest types extending 
over 26 States and Union Territories.

Ganga Action Plan 
3692. SHRI RAMACHANDRAIAH RUMANDLA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Ganga Action Plan has been reviewed; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) by when  the remaining part of the Ganga Action Plan would be  
implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Ganga 
Action Plan and the National River Conservation Plan are reviewed regul arly 
at various levels. There is a National River Conservation Authority under the 
Prime Minister which reviews the Programme. A Monitoring Committee under 
the Member, Planning Commission and a Steering Committee under Secretary, 
Ministry of Environment an d Forests review the Programme quarterly. In 
addition, a mid-term evaluation of the Ganga Action Plan Phase I was undertaken 
jointly by the Aligarh Muslim University, Roorkee University, Indian Institute 
of Technology, Kanpur and the All India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health, 
Calcutta. The evaluation report has concluded that with the reduction of 
80 

[28 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
discharge of organic matter, a necessary first step in restoring the water quality 
has been achieved to a fair level under the Ganga Action Plan Phase-I. It is also 
mentioned that the Ganga Action Plan Phase -I as conceived and implemented 
is an appropriate programme for application to other river basins. Some 
shortcomings of the programme were also brought out in the evaluation report 
and have been taken note of for suitable modification in the subsequent river 
action plan. These include reduction of discharge of organic matter, regular 
cleaning of sewage and interception structures constructed under the Ganga 
Action Plan Phase-I, regular training for the staff posted at all levels, resource 
recovery options to be analysed etc. 
A cost benefit analysis of the Ganga Action Plan phase -I was also 
undertaken by a reputed expert from Harvard Institute of International 
Development in collaboration with local Indian Institutes viz. Institute of 
Economic Growth, New Delhi Indian Toxicology Research Centre, Lucknow 
and All India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health, Calcutta. The study 
broadly concluded that inspite of its many shortcom ings the Ganga Action 
Plan Phase-I has delivered significant benefits to India. The polluted stretch of 
the river violating the bathing class standards would have been atleast 740 kms 
between Kannauj and Varanasi as compared to 437 kms between the same 
towns with the Ganga Action Plan Phase-I. In terms of both cost and time taken, 
the Ganga Action Plan Phase -I compares favourably with those of the other 
major rivers of the world. The study has concluded that the internal rate of 
return of the Ganga Action Plan Phase-I is well above 10% required of public 
sector projects. 
(c) The scheme of the Ganga Action Plan Phase- I which was started in 
1985 has been closed with effect from 31.3.2000. However, the second phase of 
the Ganga Action Plan covering rivers Yamuna, Gomati, Damodar and the main 
stem of Ganga approved between April 1993 and October 1996 is presently 
under implementation and is likely to be completed by the end of 10th Plan.

Poaching of adult male wild elephants in Orissa 
3694. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there has been large scale poaching of adult 
male wild elephants in Orissa for ivory trade since 1990; 
(b) what steps Government have taken to stop these activities; 
(c) the number of adult male wild tuskers of breeding age alive in Orissa 
at present as per the 1999 census; and 
(d) whether the male-female sex ratio of wild elephants has been severely 
damaged in Orissa? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) Yes, Sir. 103 male elephants 
have been poached in Orissa since 1990. 
(b) The steps taken by the Government to stop these activities are as 
given below: 
(i) Regular patrolling of elephant areas. 
(ii) Installation of VHF stations with mobile facility for better 
communication of protection work. 
(iii) Formation of antipoaching mobile squad. 
(iv) Installation of antipoaching checkgates at strategic and sensitive 
points. 
(v) Provision of secret funds for collection of intelligence of poachers 
and their activities. 
(vi) Elephant is included in Schedule 1 of the Wild life (Protection) Act, 
1972, which provides full protection against hunting & commercial 
exploitation. 
82 

[28 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(vii) Trade in elephant ivory has been totally banned to discourage poaching 
in elephants for its tusk. 
(viii) The Asian Elephant is also included in Appendix-1 of the Convention 
on International Trade in Endangered Species of Flora and Fauna 
(CITES) which prohibits International Trade in Asian Ivory. 
(ix) Government of India has launched Project Elephant in 1992 to provide 
impetus to the conservation of wild elephants in India. Under this 
project assistance is given to 12 states for strengthening their protection 
and communication infrastructure, development of habitat, prevention 
& mitigation of man-elephant conflicts etc. 
(c) As per recent census (1999) there are 400 adult males in Orissa. 
(d) No, Sir. As per 1979 census the sex ratio was Ml: Female 2.5 and as per 
census 1999 the sex ratio was Ml: Female 2.5.1. This indicates that there is no 
damage to sex ratio of Male-Female Elephant in Orissa.

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2000] 
(a) whether it is a fact that infant mortality rate scenario is grim in India, 
as reported in the Times of India during second week of March, 2000; and 
(b) if so, the steps taken to improve the nutritional status of the mother 
as well as child care, to improve the infant mortality rate? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) and (b) With the 
implementation of Universal Immunization Programme and the Oral 
Rehydration Therapy Programme, the infant mortality rate (IMR) has come 
down from 104 in 1985 to 72 in 1998. During the last four years, however, the 
infant mortality rate has remained in the range of 74 to 72. Under the 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme launched in 1997, a number of 
interventions are being implemented for improving the health and nutrition 
status of mothers and children. For the mothers interventions include antenatal 
and post -natal check -up, improving safe delivery paractices, prophyalix and 
treatment of maternal anemia, immunization against tetanus and promotion of 
birth spacing. The interve ntions being implemented for children include 
immunization against six vaccine preventable diseases, control of death due to 
diarrhoeal diseases and acute respiratory infections, prophylasix against Vitamin 
A deficiency blindness and nutritional anemia. Es sential Newborn Care has 
been included for reduction of deaths during the neonatal period. 
Special efforts for improving implementation of the programme are being 
planned in identified districts in 16 States of the country with the help UNICEF. 
A new proje ct for strengthening of the immunization programme with World 
Bank assistance has also been finalized. 
A National Nutritional Policy has been formulated in 1993 and the 
national plan of action on nutrition is being implemented through different 
departments of Government of India including the Integrated Child 
Development Services of the Department of Family Welfare. 
Apart from health related factors, illiteracy, poverty and general economic 
and social development of the people have a direct bearing on the i nfant 
mortality rate. To tackle these, programmes such as Jawahar Rojgar Yojana, 
Integrated Rural Development Programme, Indira Awas Yojana and Adult 
Literacy Programme are being implemented by different departments and 
agencies of Government of India.

Practicalising Policy to control Population 
3720.   SHRI M.N. DAS: 
SHRI NANA DESHMUKH:  
SHRI C.M. IBRAHIM:                
SHRI GHULAM NABIAZAD. 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are prepared to implement effective policies to 
control the population explosion; 
(b) if so, whether some policies can be made realistic and practical when 
put to operation; and 
(c) whether Government would make a new law providing five per cent 
preference in all Government jobs including IAS and IPS to those applicants 
who submit the certificate that he is the only child of his parents? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) The National 
Population ((NPP), 2000 has been approved by the Government during February, 
2000 and has been laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha on 7th March, 2000. 
Government is serious about implementing an effective policy to stabilize 
population. The policy envisages setting up of the following new structures for 
more effective review of implementation: 
(i) National Commission on Population. 
(ii) State/UT Commission on Population. 
(iii) Coordination Cell in the Planning Commission and 
(iv) Technology Mission in the Department of Family Welfare. 
(b) The policy lays down 14 National Socio- demographic goals to be 
achieved. These are: 
(1) Address the unmet needs for basic reproductive and child health 
services, supplies and infrastructure. 
(2) Make school education up to age 14 free and compulsory, and reduce 
drop outs at primary and secondary shcool levels to below 20 percent 
for both boys and girls. 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2000] 
(3) Reduce infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1000 live briths. 
(4) Reduce maternal mortality ratio to below 100 per 100,000 live births. 
(5) Achieve universal immunisation of children against all vaccine 
preventable diseass. 
(6) Promote delayed marriage for girls, not earlier than age 18 and 
preferably after 20 years of age. 
(7) Achieve 80 percent institutional deliveries and 100 perce nt deliveries 
by trainef persons. 
(8) Achieve universal access to information/counseling, and services for 
fertility regulation and contraception with a wide basket of choices. 
(9) Achieve 100 per cent registration of births, deaths, marriage and 
pregnancy. 
 
(10) Contain the spread of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS), 
and promote greater integration between the management of 
reproductive trace infection (RTI) and sexuallytransmitted infractions 
(STI) and the National AIDS Control Organisation. 
(11) Prevent and control communicable diseases. 
(12) Integrate Indian System of Medicines (ISM) in the provison of 
reproductive and child health services, and in reaching out to 
households. 
(13) Promote vigorously the small family to achieve replacement levels of 
TFR. 
(14) Bring about convergence in implementation of related social sector 
programs so that family welfare becomes a people centred program. 
In addition, Policy gives Action Plan for each of the strategies mentioned 
in the document. These action plans lead to several programs and pr ojects 
towards effective implementation of the strategies. 
These strategies are: 
(1) Decentralized planning and program implementation. 
(2) Convergence of service delivery at village levels. 
(3) Empowering women for improved health and nutrition. 
(4) Child Survival and Child Health. 
104 

[28 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(5) Meeting the unment needs for family welfare services. 
(6) Under-served population groups: 
Uban slums; 
Tribal communities, hill area population and desplaced and migrant 
populations; 
Adolescents; 
Increased participation of men in planned parenthood. 
(7) Diverse health care providers. 
(8) Collaboration with and commitments from non-government 
organizations and the private sector. 
(9) Mainstreaming Indian Systems of Medicine and Homeopathy. 
 
(10) Contraceptive technology and research on reproductive and child 
health. 
(11) Providing for the Older Population. 
(12) Information, Education and Communication. 
(c) There is no proposal to introduce legislation to provide 5 percent 
preference in Government jobs, including IAS and IPs to those applicaant 
who submit the certificate that he is the only child of his parents.

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T SHANMUGAM): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. In so far as 
HIV/AIDS is concerned, NGOs have been involved in prevention and care

106 

[28 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
As far as multi drug resistant TB is concerned, national Tuberculosis 
Control Programme encourages involvement of NGOs, private and charitable 
organisations pri vate providers at various levels. Some NGOs like Mahavir 
Hospital in Hyderabad, SEWA in Ahmedabad and R.K. Mission in Delhi etc., 
are helping in imple meeting Revised National TB Control Programme 
(RNTCP). For wider involvementof NGOs approved policy for their involvemeni 
in the RNTCP has been widely circulated. 
In the policy for NGO involvement, five schemes have been devised for 
involvement of NGOs in the RNTCP as under: 
Scheme 1: 
Includes health education and community outreach in which commodity 
assistance in the form of literature, etc. and grant -in-aid for covering training 
and incidental charges has been proposed to be given. 
Scheme 2: 
The NGOs provide Directly Observed Treatment to patients. The suppor 
will be in the form of commodity assistance and grant-in-aid which include 
Rs. 175 to the individual volunteer for each cured patient as well a 
reimbursement of incidental charges. 
Scheme 3: 
In-hospital care for tuberculosis. The hospital will follow RNTCP 
policy and will be given both commodity assistance and grant-in-aid. 
Scheme 4: 
Microscopy and treatment centre. The NGO is designated as a Microscop 
and Treatment Centre for the defined population. The commodity assistance 
will include laboratory consumables and cash assistance for civil works, gran 
in-aid and will also include incidental charges, transportation, etc. 
Scheme 5: 
Tuberculosis Unit Model the NGO will cover approximately 5 lakh 
population and will have up to five microscopy centres. Commodity 
assistance will include anti -TB drugs, microscopes and laboratory 
consumables, et Mobility of the Senior TB Supervisor (STS) and Senior TB 
Laboratoi Supervisor (STLS) will also be taken care of. The grant-in-aid will 
include funds for training as well as for civil works, etc.

STATEMENT 
Modernisation of Madarsa Education 
Under the 15 point Programme of Empowered Committee on Minorities 
Education, the Scheme of Modernisation of Madarsas on Voluntary basis is 
being implemented since 1993-94. The objective of the scheme is to encourage 
traditional institutions like Madarsas and Maktabs by giving financial assistance 
to introduce Science, Mathematics, Social Studies, Hindi and English in their 
curriculam. It is being implemented by State Governments as a Central Scheme 
under which 100% assistance is provided by the Centre. 
Under the Scheme of Modernisation of Madarsa Education, financial 
assistance for following items is given:—  
(i) One or two teachers' salary for teaching modern subjects in Madarsa 
@ Rs. 3,000/- p.m. for primary classes and Rs. 4,000/- p.m. for secondary 
classes. 
(ii) An lumsum grant of Rs. 7,000/ - for purchase of Science/Maths Kit to 
each Madarsa. 
(iii) An amount of Rs. 7,000/ - per Madarsa is granted for establishment of 
book banks and strengthening of libraries in the Madarsas for modern 
subjects. 
(iv) Any other item with the approval of Grants in aid Committee. 
The scheme is continuing during IXth Plan. An amount of Rs. 37.00 
crores has been provided during the Ninth Five Year plan for this scheme. 
The budget allocation for the current year i.e. 2000-2001 is Rs. 12.00 
Crores.

STATEMENT-II 
The Government has taken a number of measures both administrative 
and legal to prevent children from being abused. Some of which are as follows:- 
(I) LEGAL: 
The following are important specific legislations to protect the children 
from the clutches of violence and abuse meted out to them:— 
(i) Juvenile Justice Act. 1986. 
The Juvenile Justice Act, 1986 has provisions for protection from 
cruelty and has elab orate provisions for the care, protection and 
rehabilitation of neglected and abused children. The Immoral 
Prevention Act, 1956 (as amended) deals with the punitive as also 
preventive aspects of prostitution including child prostitution. 
(ii) Probation of Offenders Act, 1958. 
(iii) The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986. 
(iv) The Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of 
Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1996. 
(v) The Factories Act (Amended) 1954. 
(vi) The Child Marriage Restraint Act (Amended) 1979. 
(vii) The Orphanages and Other Charitable Homes (Surpervions & Countrol) 
Act, 1960. 
(viii) Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956. 
(ix) The Infant Milk Substitute, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods 
(Regulation of Production Supply & Offenders) Act, 1992. 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2000] 
(x) The Pre -Natal Diagnostic Technique (Regulation, Prevention and 
Misuse) Act, 1994. 
(xi) Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956. 
(2) Indian Penal Code considers the following as serious offences:—  
(i) Kidnapping or maiming a child for begging (Section 363-A-IPC). 
(ii) Selling or buying of girls for purposes of prostituion (Section 372 and 
373 IPC). 
(iii) Exposure and Abandonment of children under 12 years by parents or 
guardians (Section 317 IPC). 
(iv) Sexual harassment (Section 509), child prostitution and child rape are 
also covered. 
(II) POLICIES AND PROVISIONS 
(i) The National Policy for Children's 1974 states that "children shall be 
protected against neglect, cruelty and explotation". 
(ii) The National Decadal Plan of Action for the Girl Child 1991 -2000 
recognises the rights of the girl child to protection from exploitation, 
assault and physical abuse. 
(iii) The National Policy on Education recommends firm exclusion of 
corporal punishment to children in schools. 
(III) ADMINISTRATIVE MEASURES 
(i) The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment has also been 
implementing a scheme for welfare of street children, which has been 
reviewed and revised and renamed as An Integrated Programme fo r 
Street Children. The basic aim of the programme is to protect a children 
from all types of abuse, including rape and induction into prostitution 
etc. which they are exposed to when on the street unprotected. 
(ii) One of the important initiatives taken un der the revised scheme was 
the establishment of Child Helpline Service in a number of cities. The 
Child Helpline is a 24 hour free phone service which can be accessed 
by children in distress by dialing the number 1098 on the telephone. 
The service is currently available at Mumbai, Delhi, Calcutta, Chennai, 
Hyderabad, Nagpur, Bangalore and Patna.

to suggest measures to be taken for eradicating child prostitution. The

CAG's Concern over Rail Coaches 
3773. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Comptroller and Auditor General of India has expresse d 
concern over the falling sick of a large number of rail coaches, within three 
months of their mandatory periodic overhauling, because of poor workmanship 
over partial repairs; 
(b) if so, details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken to improve the situaiton? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The CAGs report No. 9 of 1999 mentions 
that a number of coaches are falling sick within 3 months of the periodic 
overhaul, thereby indicating poor quality attention in the workshops. 
The action taken report on this para was submitted by the Ministry of 
Railways which dispels the doubts raised by the report about coaches falling 
sick within 3 months after the overhaul. The word 'sick' is used in Railways to 
describe any coach which needs to be detached for attention at the depot repair 
facility called ""Sick Line". Sick marking of coaches is a normal part of 
maintenance and the causes of marking coaches sick are regularly analysed as 
an aid to the management to detect any adverse trends arising out of poor 
quality of workmanship, design or material. 
A new parameter of ""coaches marked sick within 100 days from the 
periodic overhaul" was devised in 1996- 97 to monitor the relative quality of 
work at different workshops. Record s indicate the numebr of coaches marked 
sick per 100 coaches overhauled has reduced from 6.4 in 1996- 97 to 5.7 in 
1998-1999, which has been possible through persistent efforts and close 
monitoring. The improvement in reliability was also evident from reduction in 
enroute coach detachments which have reduced from 361 cases in the year 
1996-97 to 197 during the year 1998-99, inspite of increased number of trains. 
It is further supported by the fact that IR have constantly maintained 
coach availability above t he prescribed 90% level. These improvements are 
results of improved attention to coaches, particularly at workshops. 
(c) Action is taken regularly to improve the areas of weaknesses revealed 
in the analysis at both manufacturing and repairs facilities. Some of the 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2000] 
important measures which have been taken by the Railways for improvement 
in workmanship and longevity of coaches are as under: 
(i) ISO certification of Coach Production Units and important Periodic 
Overhauling Workshops. 
(ii) Quality audits of Periodic Overhauling Workshops and Maintenance 
Depots. 
(iii) Strict control on the quality of output from Coach Periodic Overhauling 
Workshops through the system of Netural Examiners. 
(iv) Review and improvements of existing coach maintenance 
infrastructure and provision of new facilities for additional trains. 
(v) Design improvements and introduction of better material to improve 
reliability of coaches like Bogie mounted brakes, Composite brake 
blocks, high capacity couplings, etc. 
(vi) Broadband analysis of reliability parameters to identify weak systems, 
depots, workshops direct efforts and resources to eliminate the same. 
Besides the above improvements in existing coaches and maintenance 
system, Railways are also in the mid st of Coach Technology Upgradation 
through induction of State -of-Art coaches and transfer of technology of their 
design and manufacture.

3778. SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the National Transport Policy Committee (NTPC) had 
fixed long back the share of Rail Transport at 72% and Roadways at 28%; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that Railways are currently carrying only about 25% 
and Roadways 75%; 
(c) if not, the real situation and the basis for this data; 
(d) if so, what has been shortfall in freight traffic during 1997-98,1998-99 and 
1999-2000; and 
(e) the changes in the Budget of 2000-2001 has brought in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. The National Transport Policy Committee (NTPC) in 
1980 had allocated an optimal inter-modal mix of land freight traffic for Rail Transport 
at 72% and that of Road at 28%. 
(b) and (c) The India n Railways freight traffic was 301.52 BTKMs (revised 
estimated for 1999-2000). While Railways maintain comprehensive records of 
152 

[28 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the traffic carried by them similar data is not maintained by Roadways which is the 
other principal mode of land transport. Only some estimates prepared by 
committees/experts groups are available. These estimates are based on certain 
assumptions and may not be the actual quantum of traffic carried by Roadways. The 
latest estimates from the Planning  Commission are available only for 1995. 
According to these estimates the share of railways in the land freight traffic is about 
40%. 
It may, however, be more appropriate to compare only that portion of the land 
transport as moves over medium and long leads as rail transport is more suited for 
such leads. Adopting this approach, a recent study by RITES had estimated the rail 
share in land transportation with a lead of more than 300 Kms  as 65.6% in 1995-
96.

Network’, but a multi -pronged new Freight Policy with the following 
elements:—  
Recovering non -bulk high value traffic through appropriate 
marketing efforts. 
Providing incentives like ‘volume discount scheme’. 
Offering the leasing route to Freight Forwarders in the Luggage 
Vans (SLRs) on popular mail and express trains. 
Facilitating warehousing at existing railway terminals as a 
marketing tool to attract traffic. 
Extending the new concept of Roll -On-Roll-Off (RO -RO) in 
freight movement trucks rolled on to flat wagons will be transported by 
Rail and unloaded from wagons at destinations to provide door to door 
collection and delivery. This has been successfully launched on the 
Konkan Railway. 
Running of fixed schedule freight trains and terminal operations. 
Launching the ‘Freight Operations Information System’ (FOIS) to 
provide real-time information to customers in regard to booking,

movement and delivery of freight consignments through Customer

DKJVIJAY SINGH): (a) Yes Sir. Container Corporation of India Ltd. (CONCOR)

equipment will be used in CONCOR terminal only.

bank deposits, short -term bonds etc. on which the surplus funds of  
CONCOR are parked as per the extent guidelines.

bills of the terminal operator.

CONCOR till full recoveries have been made.

3801. SHRI W. ANGOU SINGH: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the' steps taken by Government on the recomm endation of Shukla 
Commission regarding extension of Rail line along the Chindwin Valley, parallel 
to the Mizoram Manipur Border, to link with the main Yangaon—Mandalay 
rail system of Myanmar; and 
(b) if so, by when the work would be taken up and if not, the r easons 
therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) Recommendaitons of the Shukla 
Commission on the development of North Eastern States are taken into 
consideration while formulating Railways plans for the North Eastern Region. 
Providing connection between theYangon- Mandalay rail system of Myanmar 
and the Indian Railway system is a part of the proposal for the Southern corridor 
of Trans Asia Railway. 
The proposal for developing a Railway Corridor is being pursued both 
under the aegis of Internation Union of Railways (UIC), Paris and UN-ESCAP, 
Bangkok. Ther proposed corridor seeks to link Europe/ CIS countries to 
Singapore/South East Asian countries via Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, India, 
Bangaladesh and Myanmar. Ministry of Railways has been coordinating with 
UIC and UN-ESCAP to pool their efforts and resources for synergistic approach 
on the project. 
The alignment proposed by UN -ESCAP in its recently submitted report 
on the route of the Southern Corridor of the Trans-Asian Railway from Kunming/ 
South of Bangkok to Kapikule (Bulgaria)/CIS countries passes through 
Myanmar into India. The report is under discussion by the member countries of 
UN-ESCAP. Since the project requires approval of all member countries, no 
time-frame can be given for its implementation.

SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI (Uttar Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
associate myself with what Shri Ram Gopal Yadav has said. It is a fact that a 
large number of officers are v ery hard working, industrious and have a sense 
of commitment. But, unfortunately, an impression among the people is now 
growing that a very large number of people are insensitive to the needs and 
demands of the people and sometimes, this happens, particula rly if the 
administration, that is, the political executive, does not exercise proper control 
or does not give them proper direction. I read this in a newspaper today 
morning. . There was a discussion in the House about something having 
taken place in the State of Andhra Pradesh. Similarly, many other cases 
come up. I remember, when Shri Narasimha Rao was the Prime Minister, 
there was a long discussion on the All India Service

officers. Sir, it is necessary that this ques tion should be looked into in a proper 
perspective and in a proper background. After all, nowadays, the District 
Officers have an important role to play. Then it is a changed role that he has to 
play. That is why his availability to the representatives of the people and his 
willingness to listen to the complaints of the people, should have the first 
priority. This becomes the responsibility all the more of the Central 
Government to ensure that. Whether it is an IAS officer or an IPS officer or an 
IFS officer - he has referred to IAS officers - it is they who man the district, 
who man the Secretariat usually and mostly. That is why, since it is the joint 
responsibility of the Union Government and the State Government, the 
Government of India should also be al ert and alive as to how is it that these 
complaints are becoming more and more pronounced and more and more 
frequent. If one opens a newspaper anyday, one finds such things. In Tamil 
Nadu an officer has been suspended because there was a complaint by a lady 
officer who came to make some represenation. This morning also some news 
has come. He does not belong to the IAS cadre. He belongs to some other 
service. His wife's name - I will not mention the name - has been involved in 
one of the very bad cases of non -banking financial institutions. This case has 
been going on for the last one and a half years. It is a Maple Leaf case. The 
person is not traceable while he should be working in the office. It is not a 
question of insensitivity, callousness and dis -courtesy. There are complaints 
also that somehow or the other there is lack of integrity and lack of honesty. 
This is a matter which needs serious consideration. We should not take it very 
lightly because it is the officers who form a link between the Government and 
the people as well as the representatives of the people. That is why these 
specific cases must be looked into. I think there should be a general 
discussion about this. We have been hearing of administrative reforms, 
attitudinal changes and training, etc. I have also been associated with a 
training institution for the last 25 years. They are all very important. We read 
such things in newspapers about the    State of Uttar Pradesh also. 
Twice or thrice, there was President's rule. Now it is unfortunate that 
this kind of a situation has arisen. It is heartening to note that the public feels 
that whenever they go to the District Collector, he is either inaccessible or he 
is insensitive to their demands. That means, this is corroding the very fabric of 
democracy because it is corroding the faith of the people. While I would not 
like all the officers to be painted with the same brush, I think,

there is a need for introspection amongst the officers themselves, according to 
the changing requirements. I want the Government also to look at this problem 
in the same way. 
We, as representatives, have to be fair and respectful to them. I 
think, the officers also have to reciprocate in the same manner. They should 
act in the context of people's requirements and people's needs. I would 
particularly like to mention this. This is a question of divided responsibility and 
for the All India Service Officers, this was specifically done, with a particular 
purpose, by the founding fathers of C onstitution. That is why it is necessary 
that the Government of India should also be alert and it should not say that the 
particular officer belongs to that State and thus try to evade the responsibility. 
This matter may transcend even State boundaries. It  is crucial for a 
harmonious relationship between politicians, political representatives and the 
administration. It is also a question of harmonious relationship and faith in the 
administration itself. 
Thank you very much, Sir.

Protest by Handloom Workers from Kerala 
SHRI J. CHTHARANJAN (Kerala): Hon. Chairman, Sir, I am 
extremely grateful to you for permitting me to raise certain serious problems 
affecting the handloom workers in the country. As all of us know, it is the 
oldest and traditional industry. Even now, it is engaging the largest number of 
workers in the whole country. This industry has been, for a long time, a crisis -
ridden industry. Therefore, the Government has adopted several schemes to 
protect the industry and also to help the weavers. In 1998,  the Government of 
India had appointed a Committee named the Satyam Committee which has 
submitted its Report. It is reported that the recommendations of the Report, if 
implemented, the industry will find it difficult to survive. Therefore, the matter is 
to be considered seriously by the Government. Some of the steps that have 
been taken to protect the industry and also to give relief to the handloom 
weavers are: earlier, there used to be a rebate system, but later on, instead of 
a rebate system, a marketing assistance system was introduced and then 
about 20 or 21 items of cloth were specially reserved for the handloom sector. 
And, it was decided that the mills should produce hank yarn and supply it to 
the handloom weavers. Even though all those conditions were there, 
generally, they were not properly being implemented and, in many cases, they 
were being violated. But, now, the Satyam Committee had recommended the 
giving up of almost all these schemes which were introduced to protect the 
industry and also to help the weavers. Therefore, I request, through you, the 
Government of India to reject the recommendations of the Satyam Committee 
and also seriously consider giving sufficient protection and relief to the 
handloom weavers and the industry. My suggestion is , the marketing 
assistance system, which was in vogue, should be continued. Hank yarn will 
have to be produced and supplied and the textile mills should be asked to 
provide them - even a higher count of hank yarn  and several such

met all of them on the streets of Delhi So, it shows the seriousness of the 
situation. Something adverse happened in this area. You see, what was the 
situation 4-5 years back? Starvation deaths were reported from different parts 
of the country, especially from Andhra Pradesh. Now, because of these 
recommendations, they are going to lose whatever little benefits they have 
been getting from the Government. The situation is very bad. Because of this 
new trend, new fashion, one of the oldest traditional industry of this country is 
facing a serious threat. The younger generation is normally not using 
handloom cloth. Even the people, in States like Kerala, who had been using 
dhotis, are now turning to pants. The demand for handloom cloth in the market 
is very less. So, assistance from the Government is very much needed. The 
Government should protect them by extending rebates and other assistance, 
which they had been receiving earlier. Because of these new 
recommendations, the life of these weavers is going to be more and more 
miserable. There would be starvation deaths  in villages. So, in order to avoid 
such a situation, the Government should not accept these recommendations, 
and maximum assistance should be given to the handloom weaving 
community of the country.

DR. Y. RADHAKRISHNA MURTY(Andhra Paradesh) : Sir, this 
morning, we had some discussion arising out of a Special Mention, on the 
handloom industry, but because the scope was not much and the scope for 
discussion on a Bill is much wider, I would like to go into some other aspects 
of this Bill. Also, yesterday, a delegation from all over the country had come to 
Delhi and met the Prime Minister and gave a memorandum to save the 
handloom industry because of the threat to the handloom industry  arising out 
of the recent Satyam Committee's report. 
And handloom industry is the second largest vocational activity after 
agriculture in our country. It is estimated that 125 lakh families live on 
handloom industry. If we have one family on an average co nsisting of four or 
five members, we find that roughly about a population of five crores is living on 
handloom industry. This industry is mostly in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, 
West Bengal, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Sir, this industry has a long history of 
exporting cloth to foreign countries, earning good foreign exchange and also 
producing extraordinarily high quality of handloom. For centuries together our 
artisans had been producing such a fine cloth about which people even today 
say and take pride that a saree could be put into a matchbox. Such fine 
artisans we had and such high traditions we had in our handloom industry. 
Even today we take pride in the artisans of our country. Unfortunately, now this 
industry is in a danger. I will just trace out the his tory. In 1945 itself this danger 
was thought of by the then Government and an All India Handloom Board was 
set up. In 1954, after we had attained Independence, another committee 
called Kanoongo Committee was constituted. This Committee after going into 
the intricacies of the industry, had advocated support both to the handloom 
industry as well as to the powerloom industry. After 20 years the Government 
set up another committee headed by Shri Sivaraman and this Committee was 
known as Sivaraman Committee. Then we had a committee called the Abid 
Hussain  Committee.     These  Committees  went  into the plight  of the 
238 

[ 28 April, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
handloom industry and together they recommended two particular things, one 
is reservation of 22 varieties of c loth for the handloom sector and the second 
important recommendation was with regard to the supply of hankyarn to the 
handloom industry. These were two very important recommendations made 
by the Sivaraman Committee. After taking into account all this, the Committee 
noted that for every individual who is taken into the powerloom" industry, 24 
people lose their job from the handloom industry. That is the damage that the 
powerloom had done to the handloom industry. So, this Committee had gone 
into the depth of  this matter and made their valuable recommendations along 
with these two recommendations that we have dealt with. We had also a 
policy in 1985 which the Government declared as the 1985 Policy on 
Handloom. This also resulted in the enactment of an Act call ed the 
Reservation Act which facilitated reservation of certain items for the handloom 
sector. Under this Act the hank yarn that was to be given to the handloom 
sector was categorised. After that some vested interests at that time 
approached the Supreme Co urt against these two recommendations, 1985 
Policy and the Reservation Act. But fortunately, the Supreme Court endorsed 
the position taken by the Government and the Committee. It said that the 
powerloom industry had been proliferating in spite of dampening  orders given 
by the Government. Finally the Government came in and regularised five lakh 
powerlooms in our country which had brought a lot of damage to the 
handloom industry. 
Then, after twenty years i.e., after 1974, another Committee called 
the Meera Sethi Committee was constituted. It had also recommended 
reservation of 11 varieties instead of 22 varieties. The number of items 
reserved was coming down. That is the reason why I am placing it before you. 
The earlier Committees recommended reservation of 22 varieties, but the 
Meera Sethi Committee recommended reservation of only 11 varieties to the 
handloom industry. Sir, even that was not implemented correctly. And, in 
1998, another Committee was constituted headed by one Mr. SR. Satyam. He 
was a retired S ecretary in the Ministry of Textiles. Unfortunately, had some 
other person been heading this Committee, he would have shown a little 
conscience and, probably, a little social sense. But, this Committee did not 
show that. I am sorry to say that. It had neit her the conscience nor the social 
sense which we expect from a Committee like that.   Therefore, this 
Committee had submitted its report 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 April, 2000 ] 
and, recently, the Ministry informed the House, in some other context, that the 
recommendations of this Committee are under the active consideration of the 
Ministry. The net result or the essence of the report of the Committee - some 
people have mentioned and some articles also have appeared in a number of 
newspapers - is, the report wil l ring a death- knell to the handloom sector. We 
can say that in one sentence. And, it is a wise and an intelligent arrangement 
for a funeral ceremony of the handloom sector. These are the comments 
made by some of the commentators on this Report. These things have come 
in the background of the GATT Agreement Some of the important 
recommendations are like this. The first one is, removal of every existing 
supporting system given to the handloom sector; the second one is, removal 
of reservation facility by scra pping the Reservation Act which I had mentioned 
earlier; the third important point of this Committee's recommendations is, 
removal of the existing compulsory production of hank yarn by mills, thus, 
totally starving this handloom sector due to non-availabil ity of yarn. The fourth 
point is, withdrawal of excise duty exemption. Sir, there was an exemption 
from the excise duty and now, they wanted to withdraw it. All the support 
systems are now withdrawn due to the recommendations of this Committee 
The Committee identified three types of cloth that is produced by the 
textile sector. Traditionally, we categorised this industry into co-operative 
sector, the master-weaver sector and the handloom sector. But, now, this has 
taken another type of categorisation. The c ategorisation is like this. The first 
one is, exclusively high value-added cloth that is produced; the second 
category is, medium -priced cloth that is produced; and the third one is, plain, 
low-cost cloth that is produced. That is how they have categorised the textile 
cloth that is produced. One of the recommendations, after this categorisation, 
is to see that the third category is taken up to the second category and the 
second category is taken up to the first category by improving the skills of the 
workers who are engaged in these particular sectors of industry. The 
upgradation of the skill is an uphill and a massive task, that too with no 
provision of monetary and technical support. And this Committee had no word 
about this technical support. These are th e three types of cloth produced. But, 
particularly, the third type of cloth in this categorisation is produced by the 
handloom sector. It provides clothing for the poor sections which cannot afford 
a high- priced product.     One commentator had pointed out  and I quote, 
"Despite its 
240 

[ 28 April, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
handloom buyers, the policy continues to speak of social objectives. Thus, its 
objectives are stated to be one of increasing the production of cloth of 
acceptable quality at reasonable prices t o meet the clothing requirements of 
the growing population, while keeping the employment potential in view." This 
is the objective of the previous Committee which, this Committee, has 
conveniently ignored that is, production of cloth of acceptable quality,  at 
reasonable prices, to meet the clothing requirement of the growing population, 
while keeping the employment potential in view. So, this objection of the 
previous committee has totally been forgotten, has totally been kept aside, and 
a new set of recomm endations has been provided. This is the result of free 
market competitive economy, which, probably, means survival of the fittest, 
survival of the most cunning, and survival of the richest. This is the free 
economy that we are seeing now. It has also reco mmended research and 
development, information technology - which is the obsession of the day, and 
the national handloom mart. These are another three recommendations that 
have been made, but there is no mention as to who will provide all these things 
to th is sector. No doubt, the scheme is very grand and fanciful, but it is not 
based on ground realities. It is only a starry height. Even the Government does 
not purchase handloom cloth for its own departments. That is the state of 
affairs today. The Janata Cl oth Scheme has been shelved in almost all the 
States. The welfare measures are inadequate and are not properly 
implemented. The net result is, famine deaths. In my own State, Andhra 
Pradesh, there are a number of reports regarding the famine deaths of peop le 
coming from the handloom industry. During the last few years, there have also 
been reports of suicides by the people belonging to the families of handloom 
weavers. So, in the background, my final request is, scrap the Satyam 
Committee's Report, enhance the welfare measures, revive the Janata Cloth 
Scheme, arrange the supply of hank yarn to this sector. The Bill - providing for 
a welfare fund — is very laudable. The Government should provide a core fund 
of Rs. Five crores, and suggest means of enhancing t he fund. So, these are 
the recommendations that I would like to make. With this, I support the Bill. 
Thank you very much. 
SHRI R. MARGABANDU (Tamil Nadu):Sir, I rise to support the Bill. 
The problems of handloom weavers have been felt in Tamil Nadu also. Late 
Annadurai, the doyen of the Dravidian Movement, while he was a Rajya 
Sabha Member from 1962 to 1967,   had raised his voice about the 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 April, 2000 ] 
plight of the handloom weavers. He had also suggested several measures 
which the Central Government and the State Government should adopt with a 
view to alleviating their problems. As it is said, in most places of Tamil Nadu, 
nearly 20-25 per cent of the population is engaged in handloom weaving. But 
they are not able to compete with the powerloom sector. They are not able to 
produce a fine variety so that people may be attracted to purchase handloom 
cloth. The result is, whatever they produce, is not marketed and not sold, and 
the workers are starving. In order to save them from starvat ion, the Central 
Government and the State Government must come forward with some 
measures, and reserve some items for. the handloom sector. Just as 11 items 
have been reserved for the handloom sector, in the same way, certain more 
items should be assigned to the handloom sector only, and those items should 
not be encroached upon by the powerloom sector. 
It should be specialty made available to them. The Central 
Government and the State Government should directly purchase it from them 
and market it. If it is  not marketed by the Government, subsidy should be 
there. The Government should come forward to provide a substantial price for 
these goods, to safeguard these people. As a matter of fact, the Central 
Government is providing only 2% subsidy for the purchas e through the 
National Handloom Development Corporation. 
Sir, there is a demand from the people that it should be increased to 
25%. They are also demanding the establishment of a separate bank to meet the 
financial requirements of these handloom weavers. S ir, there was one  
committee as has also been said by Mr. Radhakrishna Murty called the Mira 
Seth Committee which had recommended the setting up of a National Handloom 
Credit Fund, with a corpus of Rs. 500 crores. Sir, my request is that this should 
be set  up immediately. These poor people should be given interest -free loans; 
and also holiday period in the repayment of loans should be given to them. 
Several other measures should also be adopted to save these people. I request 
this hon. House to urge upon the Central and the State Governments to provide 
proper infrastructure and the latest technology - the absence of which is affecting 
the local textile industry - to safeguard these handloom weavers. Thank you, Sir. 
SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY(Tamil Nadu) : Sir, the Members should 
come forward to purchase handloom dresses. They are always wearing terry -
cotton or terry-loom.

suggestion. 
SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI (Tamil Na du): Sir, Tamil Nadu is the

SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI (Uttar Pradesh) : Sir, thank you for this

very important section of the community is not put to a di sadvantaged position.

go into the question of pride that we have always taken in the delicaci es and

much has been done in this regard. Frankly, Sir, you will recall that a very

with passion, with intensity and, I think, with the first -hand experience, what

us look at this industry in a broader perspective. 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 April, 2000 ] 
I also recall that the last committee, the Satyam Committee, was also 
referred to many a time in this House. At that time, the Report was not 
submitted. I have myself not seen the Report. The previous speaker, our friend 
from Andhra Pradesh, Mr. Radhakrishna Murty, has mentioned that, probabty,

of that, and I have not seen the Report either. But I can say that this officer, 
Mr. Satyam, was the Textile Secretary. I even do not know where he is at the 
moment and what he is doing. But, having known him for some time, since he 
had worked with me, I can say  that he is certainly a person with both social 
concern and social conscience. 
Having said that, I say that I have not seen the Report. Probably, he 
might have been influenced by, what he himself said, "the imperatives or the 
compulsions of globalisation."  But that simple factor should not blind us, 
should not make us oblivious, to the social and economic realities in this 
country. On the other hand, we have also to think what measures and what 
safeguards we can devise to retrieve the situation and to see that this precious 
and valuable industry is really protected. So far as the employment potential is 
concerned, if I am right, this industry, with such an immence potential, 
probably, may be next only to agriculture. Then, we have to take all measures. 
It is  also unfortunate that the Handloom Board which was set up 
years back with very laudable objectives, has got ritualised. It got -I hate to use 
the word-bureaucratised, in the sense that somehow or other, more questions 
were asked than going into the results , and the performance was ignored. I 
think, it fell into some kind of a trap, and, that is why, it has really outlived its 
utility. Something much more drastic has to be done. Ministers are taking note 
of what the hon. Members are saying. I am not aware of  the reaction of the 
Textile Ministry and the Textile Minister after having read the Report. 
But, Sir, I have seen at least two Reports on this, the Sivaraman 
Committee Report and the Mira Seth Committee Report. I think, these Reports 
were also on the right lines. Probably, they laid down the guidelines for us, by 
which we could take care of the obligations of liberalisation or the compulsions 
of liberalisation and, at the same time, strengthen the handloom industry in the 
country.

[ 28 April, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, in the first place, I do not see much of a confrontation between 
the powerloom sector and the handloom sector. The only thing is that one is 
comparatively weaker than the other. The powerloom sector has been, 
unfortunately, taken over, not by the persons who were in the powerloom 
sector or who were directly concerned with it, but by more powerful interests. 
That is why, this powerful sector should not be allowed to do the arm -twisting 
or to put the handloom sector to a disadvantage. 
Both the industries have a place, from the point of view of foreign 
market. Sir, you will recall that this industry in the Madras Presidency had 
earned a name for itself throughout the world, particularly, in the Western 
world. That is why I say when we could make it at a time when we were at a

not been able to give the proper support to the handloom industry to grow?

support the weaker and vulnerable sections and make this industry 
economically viable. Only when they are economically viable, the question of 
their vulnerability, from the point of view of social justice etc. will not be there. 
That is why I suggest that t he Government should come to the House with a 
clear policy statement, taking into account the place that this industry has 
occupied throughout the history of this country. I am afraid 1 do not find myself 
in agreement with the suggestions made by the last Committee that every kind 
of support to this industry must be withdrawn. If it is done it will be a disastrous 
step. For years we have been saying they should be given credit at cheaper 
rates, besides other concessions. I think we have to think on those li nes. Sir, I 
support the suggestions given by the Mira Seth Committee that there should 
be a National Credit Fund for them. I think this valuable suggestion has been 
taken into account in a different form by the mover of the Bill. 
Sir, withdrawal of facilit ies and concessions to this industry will cut at 
the roots of the handloom industry. This industry is, by and large, concerned 
with the poor people. It is really the workers' industry, wherein the family 
workers are not fully employed. On the one hand, we should see that no 
unnecessary burden is put on the industry, and on the other, the watchful 
Government should ensure that all kinds of concessions and facilities are 
provided to the needy sections. It should also ensure that these people 
because of their economic disparity are not exploited by the sharks who have 
now taken over the powerloom inudstry.    There also we have to 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 April, 2000 ] 
balance the two particular factors. So far as research and development is 
concerned, this is an extremely important area and this was supposed to be 
one of the responsibilities for the handloom industry. I would like to state that 
most of the State Governments and Departments dealing with handloom 
industry have failed in the area of research and development. Research and 
Development is extremely important, from the point of view of quality, and 
quality has something to do with marketing. Apart from that, we have to explore 
new markets for this industry. 
Then, suggest to these poor people, who are depr ived of those 
facilities, what kind of a cloth they should make, what kind of a design they 
should adopt and so on. I think this task has been neglected, though, I am not

That is why I think that another very important area which needs to be 
focussed is research and development, in order to improve their quality, 
improve their marketing prospects. Only then, they can face competition; and 
produce handloom cloth according to the taste of the people. Mr. Vice-
Chairman, without taking much of your time, I would like to submit that there is

don't want synthetic clothes. On the other hand, handloom articles are a rage in 
the Western countries. When we go abroad, we give small presents to the 
people. They are accepted. They are highly welcomed. I  think, these factors 
also should be taken into account. The easy path that we sometimes adopt is 
not something which really behoves this country with such hory traditions of 
handloom industry. 
Sir, I fully agree with the proposal for handloom mart . This is also one 
of the ways and methods of publicising the handloom ; and many efforts have 
been made in this direction, very successfully, though, in a limited way, for 
small-scale industries at different places. So far as the handloom industry is 
concerned, this is a kind of facility which the Government has not provided. If 
they provide this facility to this sector, then, we can say that they have really 
discharged their duty to this sector. Mr. Reddy, the Mover of the Bill, has 
suggested a Handloom Weavers'  Welfare Fund , on the lines of the 
Development Fund, National Credit Fund,  suggested by the Mira  Seth 
Committee.   Yes, I am for a Handloom

Weavers' Welfare Fund. But our economic policy, our industrial policy, should

approach to make the handloom industry viable can be adopted.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN) : Mr. Vice -Chairman, Sir, I am grateful to the 
Members of this House who have participated in the discussion and have 
given their suggestions about the problems of the handloom weavers. They 
are facing many difficulties in their field. I appreciate all the Members who 
have participated in the debate and given their valuable ideas and 
suggestions. 
I would like to say one thing. Handloom is a State subject. The State 
Government is fully responsible for implementing the schemes. The 
Government of India is supporting the State Governments, providing so many 
schemes and giving funds for helping the weavers. Now, our hon. friend has 
introduced a Bill. He is seeking the support of the House. He has mentioned in 
this Bill about the non-availability of yarn, assured availability of yarn at 
concessional rates, welfare m easures for the weavers, purchase of handloom 
products by the Governments, loan facilities for the weavers, constitution of an 
expert task force and other things. I would like to bring to the notice of this 
House that the Government is aware of the problem s of handloom weavers. 
The Hank Yarn Obligation Order expired on 31th March, 2000. But our 
Government issued an order extending its period without specifying any date. I 
would also like to bring to the notice of the House that, according to this Order, 
the production of hank yarn must be 50

per cent of the total production of yarn by the industry. It is compulsory. Out of 
this hank yarn, 80 per cent should be 40 counts or below. Many Members

submitted its report to the Government. We are carefully considering each

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 April, 2000 ] 
5.00 P.M. 
STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Match- Fixing in Cricket 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION AND MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI 
SUKH DEV SINGH DHJNDSA): The iss ue of match-fixing has been at the 
centre-stage of media reporting for the last few weeks. It has also been 
debated in the two Houses of Parliament. I have already made statements in 
both the Houses of Parliament on this issue. In my statement, I had menti oned 
that Government will not hesitate to initiate an inquiry in the matter of match-
fixing by any agency of the Government, as required. On the basis of several 
news-items in prominent magazines and newspapers of the country, as also 
the statement of prominent cricket administrators and players, there is need to 
inquire into the matter further. Government believes that those who are guilty 
must be punished, those who are innocent must not be slandered, those who 
have evidence must cooperate and shall be gi ven adequate protection, and 
those who make ill founded allegations must be exposed. Keeping in view the 
sentiments expressed by hon. Members in both Houses of Parliament, the 
sensitivity of the case and the complexities involved, as also the issue of 
jurisdiction, Government has decided to entrust the matter to CBI for 
appropriate inquiry and necessary action. During the discussions in Parliament 
on this issue, the pre-dominant view was also to entrust this inquiry to the CBI. 
It is hoped that this inquiry  will clear the air of rumours and suspicion 
surrounding this subject. The case already registered by the Delhi Police under 
FIR No. 111/2000 against Hansie Cronje and others will be pursued by Delhi 
Police to its logical conclusion.
